text: Initial compromise is almost never the actual goal — it's a foothold. What turns one phished laptop into a full breach is lateral movement: using what was gained at that foothold to reach further, higher-value systems. This lesson covers three real techniques attackers use to do it, and the specific controls built to stop each one, because generic advice like "segment your network" means a lot more once you can see exactly what it's segmenting against.

Pass-the-hash extracts a cached credential hash from a compromised machine, often from memory, and reuses it directly to authenticate elsewhere, without ever needing the real password. It works because many protocols accept the hash itself as proof, and because that hash is often valid everywhere — if every workstation shares the same local admin account and password, one dumped hash unlocks all of them. Token and ticket theft works differently: it steals an already-issued session token and replays it, sidestepping MFA entirely, since MFA happened once at login and the token is just proof that it happened.

The third technique is the most mundane and often the most effective: the same local administrator credentials, or one overprivileged service account, shared across large numbers of machines. Compromise one, and an attacker inherits every system that credential also controls — which is exactly how a blast-radius estimate turns out to be far larger than anyone intended.

Each technique has a specific control, not a generic one. Unique per-machine local admin passwords and Credential Guard close pass-the-hash, because a dumped hash stops being valid anywhere else. Continuous access evaluation and shorter token lifetimes close token theft, because a stolen token stops being treated as permanent proof. And credential tiering — separating domain, server, and workstation admin credentials — enforced through Privileged Access Workstations closes the shared-credential path, by keeping privileged logins off the everyday devices that get compromised most often.

None of these controls works alone. Unique admin passwords don't touch token theft; PAWs don't stop movement between two ordinary workstations on a flat network — that's what segmentation from Chapter 3 closes. The real defense is always a specific control matched to a specific technique, layered together. Next lesson takes the last step: designing the automated isolation that responds to all of this fast, as a last resort behind a human decision, not the default first move.
